stem.text: What is it called when a consumer's marginal utility is greater than the price paid for the good?

explanation.text: Consumer surplus is the gap between what a consumer is willing to pay (measured by marginal utility, converted into money terms) and what they actually pay (the price). Whenever marginal utility exceeds price, the consumer gains this extra satisfaction for free — that gain, summed across all units bought, is consumer surplus.

optionAnalysis.text: A Giffen good is a specific type of inferior good where quantity demanded rises as price rises — a demand-curve classification, not a measure of utility relative to price.
An inferior good is one whose demand falls as income rises — again a classification of the good, not a utility-price comparison.
Consumer surplus is exactly the excess of a consumer's valuation (marginal utility, in money terms) over the price actually paid.
Producer surplus is the mirror concept on the supply side: the excess of price received over the minimum price (marginal cost) a producer would accept — not about marginal utility at all.

reasoningChain: Recall that marginal utility reflects how much satisfaction, in money-equivalent terms, a consumer gets from one more unit.
When that money-equivalent value exceeds the price actually paid, the consumer has gained more than they spent.
This gap, summed over all units consumed, is defined as consumer surplus.

inferredMistakes.text: Confusing this utility-price gap with producer surplus, which is the equivalent concept on the supply side rather than the demand side.
